html:
The Bedouin are Arab nomadic herders of the deserts of Arabia, the Levant, Mesopotamia and North Africa. On this map they fill a wide stretch of the eastern Sahara, between Libya, Egypt and today's Chad and Sudan, in 900.

Their way of life rests on the camel, which can go days without water and carries people, goods and milk across the desert. They move between wells and seasonal pastures in tribal groups, and value hospitality, honour and kinship.

The Bedouin came from the Syrian and Arabian deserts. After the Arab conquests of the 7th century, tribes moved west into Egypt and beyond. By 900, Arab herders were spreading along the desert edges west of the Nile and south toward Nubia and Darfur, mixing with Berber and other Saharan peoples. A much bigger wave came in the 11th century, when the Fatimids sent the Banu Hilal into North Africa. Bedouin guided and protected the caravans of the trans-Saharan trade, and they spread Arabic across the region. Their neighbours to the south included Christian Nubia.
